Many of the previous findings and literatures have been references and discussed in the discussion.
However, it is not obvious where the novelty of this manuscript lies. This remains my major concern that
needs to be clarified before addressing my other specific questions.
We thank the reviewer for this critical point. We apologize for not making the novelty and mechanistic
insights of our study sufficiently clear in the original submission.
First, to directly address the question: our findings demonstrate that Cav1 is functionally required to
spatially restrict RhoA activation during migration through its role as a mechanosensor that dynamically
transitions between caveolae and non-caveolar scaffolds. This is not merely a phenotype of Cav1 loss but
a regulated, context-specific function of Cav1 structures. In particular:
1) At the cell front, we show that Cav1 scaffolds inhibit RhoA activation, preventing unwanted
contractility and allowing for protrusive activity.
2) At the cell rear, intact caveolae serve a mechanosensitive role by locally modulating RhoA activity
in response to tension changes.
3) This functional compartmentalization is lost in Cav1 KO cells, leading to mislocalized RhoA
activation, loss of directional migration, and failure to respond appropriately to membrane
tension cues.
We also provide causal evidence by using optogenetic tools to recruit specific RhoA GEFs (ARHGEF11/25)
and a negative control GEF (Tiam1), and we demonstrate that the inhibitory interaction between Cav1
scaffolds and RhoA is specific and spatially regulated. This further supports the conclusion that
Cav1 scaffolds actively inhibit GEF signaling at the cell front, rather than this being a passive
consequence of Cav1 absence.
Regarding novelty, we would like to clarify that:
1. Cav1 polarization has been observed (Refs. 21–24, including our own work, Ref. 22), but its
functional role has remained unknown.
2. This is the first study to demonstrate that polarized Cav1 exists in distinct structural states
(scaffolds vs. caveolae) at front vs. rear, which exert opposing effects on RhoA signaling during
migration.
3. We identify for the first time that ARHGEF25 and ARHGEF11 are spatially regulated by Cav1, with
distinct interactions at the leading and trailing edges.
4. While Cav1 scaffolds were described morphologically by the Nabi and Hamarneh groups in 2018
(Ref. 11), no mechanical or functional role had previously been attributed to these structures.
5. We now show that the caveolae-Cav1 scaffold balance is sensitive to local membrane tension
(supported by Flipper-TR probe data, new Figure 2), and that their dynamics are essential for
tuning localized signaling during migration.
Together, these findings reveal a novel mechanism by which mechanosensitive Cav1 assemblies regulate
cell migration via spatial control of RhoA signaling—a process previously uncharacterized. Notably,
whereas earlier studies have primarily focused on the role of caveolae at the rear of migrating cells, our
study uncovers a distinct function for Cav1 scaffolds at the front. We hope this clarifies the novelty and
significance of our work and are grateful to the reviewer for the opportunity to strengthen our manuscript.

This statement is supported by both qualitative and quantitative data. Specifically, in Fig.1d-h and the

We provide supporting evidence in Fig. 3a and Supplementary Video 5, which demonstrate that hypo-

quantitative analyses in Extended Data Fig. 2b comparing cell migration under Iso, hypo, and Rec

Point 5. In Fig. 3f, the quantification of PLA intensity is not acceptable, as the intensity depends on the
amplification level. However, the number of PLA dots reflects the interaction strength.
We fully agree with the reviewer that PLA signal quantification is commonly performed by counting
individual fluorescent spots, and this is the approach we have used in previous studies (Zanin et al, Nat.
Cell Biol. 2023). In this case, however, we encountered significant challenges with spot counting due to
the presence of both small, distinct puncta and larger fluorescent structures. These larger signals likely
result from the merging of closely spaced PLA puncta, compounded by the limited spatial resolution of
conventional confocal microscopy. As a result, spot-based quantification severely underestimated the
actual signal, producing values inconsistent with the corresponding images.
To overcome this limitation, we opted for fluorescence intensity quantification, which provided results
that more accurately reflected the observed signal patterns. Notably, intensity-based PLA quantification
is also an established method in other contexts, including flow cytometry applications.
To validate our approach, we contacted the manufacturer of our PLA kit (Navinci), who confirmed that
intensity-based analysis is appropriate under conditions where signals cluster or overlap. Their guidance
is as follows:
“For quantification in cells and tissues: We have found that counting signals works well when they are
scattered, as they are very easy to distinguish from each other. However, in the case of grouped signals,
it is not possible to quantify the exact number of signals in each group… We therefore recommend
13
quantifying the intensity per signal to take account of both area and intensity, so that the grouped
signals have more weight than the individual signals.
Measuring only signal intensity and not counting the signal can work if you have very uniform staining
between cells and images, and very little difference between background autofluorescence. “
Given this feedback, and to ensure consistency, we used the same quantification approach for all PLA
experiments in this study.

methods used to detect active RhoA in each panel:
• Figure 5a shows fixed-cell immunofluorescence using a mouse-monoclonal anti-RhoA-GTP antibody
(New East Biosciences, Cat. #26904), which captures a static snapshot of RhoA-GTP distribution at
the cell front and rear.
• Fig. 5e, on the other hand, presents live-cell imaging using a RhoA-biosensor (HaloTag-3xrGBD;
Addgene #176108, Mahlandt et al. J. Cell Sci. 2021, eLife 2023), which reports dynamic changes in

We respectfully disagree with the reviewer’s characterization of the RhoA biosensor signal in Fig. 5e as
“cytoplasmic”. The haloTag-3xrGBD biosensor transiently localizes to the plasma membrane upon RhoA
activation and returns to the cytoplasm upon inactivation. As shown in the original biosensor

and tightly coupled to specific cellular events such as contraction. Thus, the observed pattern in Fig. 5e
reflects the dynamic and transient nature of RhoA-GTP accumulation at the plasma membrane during cell
migration, rather than a steady-state membrane enrichment captured in fixed samples.

Point 7. The authors used the Z-shaped micropattern to capture changes in migration direction. Why not
use the well-developed PA-Rac1 optogenetic system (Yi I. Wu, 2009) to manipulate the migration direction
and record the caveolae formation?
We thank the reviewer for the suggestion and the reference to the PA-Rac1 optogenetic system developed
by Yi I. Wu et al. (2009), which is indeed a powerful tool for inducing membrane ruffling and protrusion
through localized Rac1 activation. However, the rationale behind our experimental design was to analyze
the dynamics of caveolae and RhoA signaling during spontaneous or geometrically constrained changes
in migration direction—without perturbing upstream regulators such as Rac1, which are known to cross-
regulate RhoA activity.
Importantly, manipulation of Rac1 using PA-Rac1 could confound the interpretation of RhoA-dependent
processes by disrupting the intrinsic Rho/Rac balance. Our goal was to study caveolae remodeling and
RhoA activation in response to natural or geometry-forced directional changes. To this end, we used Z-
shaped micropatterns, which allow cells to undergo directional reorientation in a controlled, reproducible
manner without the need for pharmacological or optogenetic stimulation.
Moreover, we did employ optogenetics in our study— but specifically to locally manipulate RhoA rather
than Rac1. For this, we used a well-established light-inducible dimerization system (iLID/SspB) to control
the spatial activation of RhoA and analyze Cav1 dynamics in response to localized contractile events
(Guntas et al., PNAS, 2015; Mahlandt et al., eLife 2021).
The Z-shaped micropattern system was chosen to complement other settings used in our study, including
1D-line micropatterns, 2D and 3D collagen migration assays, and optogenetically induced direction
changes (see Fig. 1, Fig. 6 and Extended Data Figs. 7-8). Together, these approaches support our central
conclusion regarding the spatiotemporal coupling of RhoGEFs and Cav1 during directional migration.
Finally, we note that Reviewer#1 explicitly appreciated the Z-shaped micropattern design and its
relevance to our study. We believe this system provides a non-invasive, geometry-driven method to probe
directional migration and associated signaling events, without introducing potential artifacts from
upstream signaling interference.

the authors show that caveolae accumulate at the rear end of cells, and that interfering with caveolae
impairs migration. Then, they show that manipulating membrane tension with osmotic shocks impairs
both the caveolin localization, and migration. This is related to RhoA, which is more active at the rear of
cells, where caveolae localize. Biochemical experiments are then used to show that RhoA interacts with
caveolin and does so preferentially when it is not within caveolae structures. Interestingly, it is caveolae
structures, rather than caveolin, that enable the cell actomyosin contractions at the rear that are necessary
for migration. Elegant photoactivation experiments then show that this is mediated by Rho GEFs. Finally,
the authors show that an increase in caveolin recruitment precedes RhoA activation when cells contract.
Overall, the data support a model in which higher membrane tension at the cell migrating front
disassembles caveolae, whereas caveolae remain formed at the rear. Rho GEFs interact with caveolae,
triggering actomyosin contraction and promoting migration. This framework is nicely supported by a
computational model. Overall, this is an elegant and thorough study, which reveals a new mechanism
regulating cell migration and coupling it to membrane tension. I therefore recommend publication, after
addressing a few important points noted below.
We sincerely thank the reviewer for their thoughtful and generous summary of our work. We greatly
appreciate the recognition of the conceptual framework and the experimental depth, particularly the
integration of mechanobiology, cell polarity, and live cell optogenetics approaches to elucidate the role
of caveolae in cell migration. In the revised version, we have endeavored to strengthen the significance
of our data with new controls and experiments.
Point 1. My main concern is that membrane tension is central to the proposed mechanism, but it is not
measured, and it is only manipulated through osmotic shocks, which can have many side effects. The
authors should either provide an alternative method to manipulate membrane tension (for instance, via
cell confinement) or some measurement of membrane tension, for instance through the flipper-TR probe.
We thank the reviewer for this important point. To directly address the concern regarding membrane
tension measurement and its role in the proposed mechanism, we performed additional experiments
using two complementary approaches:
1. Flipper-TR probe (Colom et al. Nat Chem. 2018) We used fluorescence lifetime imaging (FLIM)
Flipper-TR TR in WT Hs578t cells under under iso-osmotic conditions (Iso). As shown in Figure 2, we
observed a significant front-rear membrane tension gradient in Flipper-TR lifetimes with a higher
tension at the front and a lower one at the rear of migrating cells (panel c). This observation is
consistent with recent findings (Shi et al., Cell 2018; De Belly et al., Cell 2023; García-Arcos et al.,
bioRxiv 2024) and aligns with the observed front-rear polarity of caveolae, characterized by a
predominance of budded caveolae at the rear and Cav1 scaffolds at the front, as revealed by super-
resolution microscopy (Fig. 5 a-b).

2. Optogenetic manipulation of membrane tension using Opto-PI3K: To further validate this
mechanism using an independent approach, we now include new data from WT Hs578t cells
expressing Opto-PI3K (Fig. 2h-i). Local recruitment of Opto-Pi3K to the cell rear led to Rac-mediated
filopodia formation (Cyan line) and an increase in cell area within the opto-ROI (grey line), consistent
with a localized increase in membrane tension (De Belly et al Cell 2023). This was subsequently
followed by a decrease in Cav1 intensity (orange line), indicating caveolae disassembly. These results
directly support our model that membranae tension gradients regulate caveolae dynamics and Cav1
scaffolds distribution, and thereby influence cell polarity and directionality.

Together, these new data—based on both quantitative membrane tension measurements (Flipper-TR)
and localized mechanical perturbation (Opto-PI3K)—strongly support a mechanistic role for membrane
tension in regulating front-rear caveolae polarity. These findings have been incorporated into the revised
manuscript and are discussed in detail.
Point 2. Model: the proposed model is very interesting, but its only experimental validation seems to be
fig. 7d. First, the authors should clearly specify the values of the parameters used, and exactly which
parameters change and how in the “with feedback” and “without feedback” curves. Second, the authors
should more broadly compare model to experiments. For instance, predicted trajectories (as in fig. 7c)
could be compared to experiments, in terms of movement but also of predicted membrane tension on both
sides (which could be compared to caveolin intensity for instance, as they are predicted to follow each
other). I understand that the model is simplified and that we can’t expect a one-to-one comparison with
experiments, but still the conceptual agreement between model and experimental trends could be
explored much more broadly.
We thank the reviewer for this insightful comment and have taken steps to address both points in the
revised manuscript.
